authoring.value: Let $v_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $v_2=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\end{pmatrix}$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A$. Form $P=(v_1\ v_2)$ using these columns in this order, with their displayed scales unchanged. For the differential equation $x'(t)=Ax(t)$, define the new coordinates by $u(t)=Dx(t)$ where $D=P^{-1}$. Find the exact matrix $D$.
authoring.rationale: Specify the coordinate direction u=Dx, exact ordered eigenvector-column matrix P and unchanged eigenvector scales so D=P^-1 is unique; generic decoupling matrices remain nonunique. authoring.value:
Use the given eigenvectors as the columns of $P$ in the stated order and with their shown scales:

$$P=(v_1\ v_2)=\begin{pmatrix}1&-3\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det P=1\cdot2-(-3)(-1)=-1.$$

The requested coordinate map is $u=Dx$ with $D=P^{-1}$. The inverse formula gives

$$D=\frac{1}{-1}\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-3\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Both $DP$ and $PD$ are the identity matrix, so this is the exact inverse. If $Av_i=\lambda_i v_i$, then $AP=P\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ and

$$u'=P^{-1}Ax=P^{-1}APu=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)u.$$

The opposite coordinate direction is $x=Pu$, whose matrix is $P$, not $D$. Fixing column order and eigenvector scales is necessary to specify this exact inverse. For example, $-D$ also yields a decoupled system if one instead uses the rescaled coordinates $\widetilde u=-u$, but it is not $P^{-1}$ for the specified $P$. The original generic phrase “the decoupling matrix” did not state these conventions. The clarified prompt makes the exact inverse unambiguous; the source accepted this inverse as option c.
